newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: China envoy says Beijing backs Korea talks -Yonhap.
newsitem.headline: China envoy says Beijing backs Korea talks -Yonhap.

text.p: China's envoy to Seoul said Beijing was ready to join four-way talks involving the two Koreas and the United States to bring peace to the Korean peninsula, Yonhap news agency reported on Sunday.
The reported remarks represent Beijing's first unambiguous support for the talks proposed in April by U.S. President Bill Clinton and South Korean head of state Kim Young-sam.
They come at a critical juncture with inter-Korea relations in crisis after a North Korean submarine incursion and Pyongyang's threat to abandon a key nuclear accord.
"China takes a positive view of the four-way talks and plans to participate in the talks if related nations can reach an accord," Yonhap quoted ambassador Zhang Tingyan as saying.
Until now Beijing has been non-commital on the talks, saying only it was ready to cooperate with other countries to maintain peace and stability on the Korean peninsula.
The talks are aimed at replacing a truce that ended the 1950-53 Korean War with a permanent peace arrangement.
"China hopes peace will be established through four-way talks and it will continue to play a constructive role in the process," Zhang was quoted as saying.
Pyongyang has yet to respond to the invitation, but has long been holding out for direct peace talks with Washington, bypassing Seoul.
The agency said Zhang made his remarks in an interview to be aired later on Sunday by Yonhap Television News.
Zhang also said "peace and stability on the Korean peninsula should be accomplished through bilateral talks between South and North Korea".

It was not immediately clear how those comments squared with his support for four-way talks. However, as envisaged the four-party talks would mainly involve the two Koreas with the United States and China playing a supporting role.

"The truce treaty should be replaced with a new peace agreement through bilateral talks but the truce accord should be maintained until the peace agreement is established," Zhang was quoted as saying.
That comment was an apparent shot at North Korea, which has called the armistice a "worthless scrap of paper".

In October Beijing supported a United Nations Security Council resolution expressing serious concern over the incursion by a North Korean submarine onto a South Korean beach in September and calling on North Korea to respect the armistice.
Seoul has halted all contacts with the North until Pyongyang apologises over the submarine incident, delaying implementation of a 1994 nuclear accord between the United States and North Korea.
Under the accord, Pyongyang agreed to freeze its nuclear weapons programme in return for light-water nuclear reactors financed largely be South Korea.
On Friday Pyongyang accused Washington of dragging its heels on implementing the agreement and threatened to end its nuclear freeze.
Zhang dismissed speculation that North Korea, facing severe food shortages, was on the verge of collapse.

"It is true that North Korea suffers from economic difficulties but the North Korean regime is not going to collapse in the near future and North Korean leaders will find a solution to overcome the economic difficulties," he said. "North Korean leaders are well aware of world affairs and North Korea is changing internally.

"A military collision on the Korean peninsula is unlikely because relevant countries, including China, the United States and Japan do not want it and because North Korea well recognises this," Zhang said.
